html:
The Imamate of Futa Jallon was an Islamic state of the Fula people in the Fouta Djallon highlands of what is now Guinea, from the 1720s to 1896. The map shows it in 1880 and 1900.

The state grew out of the Fula jihad of the 1720s, led by the scholar Karamokho Alfa, in which Muslim Fula herders and their allies took power from the older farming peoples. It was ruled from Timbo by an almamy, chosen in turn from two branches of the founding family, with provincial chiefs below.

Futa Jallon became a centre of Islamic learning. Its wealth rested on cattle and on captives, many sold to the coast for the Atlantic slave trade and many more kept to farm. Its example inspired later jihads in Futa Toro and beyond. France signed protection treaties in the 1880s and took full control in 1896.
